Mathematical Foundations¶

This chapter explains the ideas that make GAMs work — not just the equations, but why we chose each ingredient and what problem it solves. linGAM ships two engines that solve the same problem with different machinery, so the chapter is organised in four parts:

  • Part I — the shared ideas both backends agree on: what a GAM is, and how its additive decomposition works.

  • Part II — the pygam backend: uniform B-splines, difference penalties, a discrete grid search over \(\lambda\), and the SVD solver. Everything you need to read the code in lingam/pygam/.

  • Part III — the mgcv backend: the basis families of R’s mgcv (thin plate, cubic, cyclic, P-splines…), the sum-to-zero identifiability constraint, and automatic smoothing-parameter selection by REML or GCV. Everything you need to read lingam/mgcv/.

  • Part IV — an explicit side-by-side comparison of the two, so you can pick the right engine for your problem.

If you’re new to GAMs, start from the top. If you already know penalised B-splines, skip to the SVD solver (pygam) or the mgcv bases, and finish with the comparison.

Part I — Shared foundations¶

Why GAMs?¶

Classical linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane):

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \dots + \varepsilon_i.\]

The problem: the real world is rarely a straight line. Temperature does not degrade turbine blades linearly. Dose-response curves saturate. An engine’s sweet-spot RPM is a peak, not a slope.

Generalised Additive Models replace each linear term \(\beta_j x_{ij}\) with a learned smooth function \(f_j(x_{ij})\):

\[y_i = \beta_0 + f_1(x_{i1}) + f_2(x_{i2}) + \dots + \varepsilon_i.\]

Now the model can bend to match the data. The word additive means the contributions still sum together — there’s no multiplicative or nested structure, just a collection of understandable pieces you can inspect one at a time. The word generalised means we replaced “linear coefficient × predictor” with “learned function of predictor.”

This is the central tradeoff of statistical modelling:

Simple models (lines) don’t capture reality. Complex models (deep nets, random forests) capture it but you can’t explain how. GAMs sit in the sweet spot: flexible enough to fit nonlinear patterns, interpretable enough that each term is a plot you can show to a colleague.

When you call model.plot_decomposition(x, y), what you see is the decomposition of the prediction into independent pieces:

\[\hat y(\mathbf{x}) = \underset{\text{intercept}}{\beta_0} + \underset{\text{term 0}}{f_1(x_1)} + \underset{\text{term 1}}{f_2(x_2)} + \dots + \underset{\text{noise}}{\hat\varepsilon}.\]

Each subplot in the decomposition is one \(f_j\) in isolation. Because the model is additive, the pieces are independent: changing \(x_1\) only affects \(f_1(x_1)\), not \(f_2(x_2)\). This is the property that makes GAMs interpretable where black-box models are not.

Both linGAM backends fit exactly this model. Where they differ is how: how each \(f_j\) is represented, how the smoothness penalty is built, how the smoothing parameter is chosen, and how uncertainty is reported. Part II and Part III cover those differences; the shared philosophy is the equation above.

Decomposition: how the model explains its predictions¶

The defining feature of GAMs is that predictions decompose additively:

\[\hat y(\mathbf{x}_i) = \underbrace{\hat\beta_0}_{\text{intercept}} + \underbrace{\hat f_1(x_{i1})}_{\text{term 1}} + \underbrace{\hat f_2(x_{i2})}_{\text{term 2}} + \dots + \underbrace{\hat f_p(x_{ip})}_{\text{term p}}.\]

Each \(\hat f_j\) is a partial dependence function — it shows how the prediction changes when you vary \(x_j\) while holding everything else fixed (usually at the median). This is the “all else equal” effect.

The plot_decomposition grid. When you call model.plot_decomposition(x, y), you see:

  • Top row — overall fit: The model’s prediction when sweeping the first predictor across its range, with all others at their medians. Gray dots are the actual data. This gives you a quick sanity check: does the curve pass through the cloud of points?

  • Per-term panels: One subplot for each term in the formula:

    • s() panel: a line plot. The curve shows how blade life changes with temperature (or RPM, or vibration). A flat line means the term contributes nothing — the predictor doesn’t matter. A steep curve means the predictor is important.

    • te() panel: a 2-D heatmap (or projection line for 3+D). Blue = below-average contribution, red = above-average. Look for diagonal patterns — they indicate synergy. A uniform color means no interaction.

    • f() panel: a bar chart. Each bar is one category’s baseline shift relative to the reference level. Tall bars mean big differences between categories.

    • l() panel: a straight line. The slope (beta coefficient) is shown in the title. The line passes through zero at the median of the predictor.

  • Red shaded regions: Extrapolation — the model is predicting outside the range of the training data. Treat these regions with caution; the linear extrapolation used there is a heuristic, not a guarantee.

  • Zero reference lines: Each term’s contribution is centred so that the sum of all contributions (plus intercept) equals the prediction. The dashed horizontal line at zero shows where the term contributes nothing.

How to read the decomposition as a story. Start from the leftmost term and work right. Each panel answers one question:

  1. “What does temperature do to blade life, all else equal?”

  2. “What does RPM do, all else equal?”

  3. “Do temperature and vibration interact synergistically?”

  4. “Does coating type A last longer than B?”

  5. “Is cooling flow linearly protective?”

The answers are independent — they add up to the full prediction, but you can understand each one without reference to the others. This is the superpower of additive models: complex predictions built from simple, understandable pieces.

Partial dependence vs. raw data. The partial dependence curves do NOT show the raw data distribution; they show the model’s isolated view of each predictor. A scatter of raw data against a single predictor mixes in the effects of all other predictors, so it can look very different from the partial dependence. The partial dependence is the “clean” signal — the model’s best estimate of what that predictor alone contributes.

One subtlety to remember later: the two backends centre these term plots differently. The mgcv backend enforces an explicit sum-to-zero constraint on every smooth (so each panel is genuinely centred at zero), while the pygam backend lets the intercept absorb each term’s overall level. We’ll make this precise in Part III.

Part II — The PyGAM backend¶

How the pygam backend thinks¶

The pygam backend (backend='pygam') is the minimalist design: one basis family, one solver, one criterion, chosen well. Every smooth term is a uniform cubic B-spline; smoothness is charged by a difference penalty; the one free knob, the smoothing parameter \(\lambda\), is chosen by evaluating a discrete grid of candidates and keeping the one with the best Generalised Cross Validation (GCV) score.

The whole pipeline is:

\[\text{formula} \;\to\; \underbrace{B\text{-spline bases } X}_{\S 1} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{penalty } P}_{\S 2} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{solve } (X^\top X + P)\hat\beta = X^\top y}_{\S 3--4} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{score with GCV, pick best } (K, \lambda)}_{\S 5--6}.\]

Each step is a section below. The design bets on three ideas:

  1. Uniform B-splines are good enough. A cubic B-spline with 10–20 basis functions can approximate almost any smooth engineering relationship; the exact knot placement rarely matters at that resolution.

  2. Grid search is honest. Instead of optimising \(\lambda\) continuously (which requires derivatives of criteria that may have flat or multiple minima), evaluate a finite, user-visible grid and pick the winner. Slow in theory, fast in practice once you precompute cleverly (grid search).

  3. SVD is the safest solver. Never form \(X^\top X\) explicitly; work with a square-root of the penalised system instead (SVD solver).

Identifiability in this backend is implicit: the intercept column is unpenalised and absorbs the overall level, and each penalty leaves its own null space (constant and linear trends for the default penalty) uncharged, so the decomposition into intercept + smooths is well defined in practice. There is no explicit centering constraint — a deliberate simplification we compare against mgcv’s approach later.

B-spline bases: building curves from building blocks¶

If we want \(f(x)\) to be a smooth, flexible curve, we need a way to represent it mathematically.

Why not just use a high-degree polynomial? A degree-20 polynomial can wiggle a lot, but when you fit it to data every point in one corner of the plot affects the curve everywhere. You get wild oscillations (Runge’s phenomenon). Polynomials are globally coupled — change one coefficient and everything changes.

The key insight of B-splines: build the curve from localised building blocks. Each block (basis function) is nonzero only in a small region. Adjusting a block only changes the curve in its neighbourhood, not across the whole domain. This is called compact support.

Think of LEGO bricks. A long, curved wall isn’t built from one flexible piece — it’s built from many small, rigid bricks each responsible for a tiny segment. The bricks overlap slightly at the edges for smoothness. B-spline basis functions are the mathematical equivalent: each one is a smooth “bump” that covers a few neighbouring data points. When you stack them with different heights (coefficients \(\beta_j\)), you get any smooth shape you want:

\[f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^K \beta_j \, B_j(x).\]

Each \(B_j(x)\) is one basis function; \(\beta_j\) is how tall you make it; \(K\) is how many bricks you use (n_splines in the API).

The De Boor recursion. A B-spline of order \(k\) (polynomial degree \(k-1\)) is built recursively. Given data \(x \in [x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\), we map to \([0, 1]\):

\[z = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}.\]

Uniform interior knots divide \([0, 1]\) into segments:

\[\tau_0 = 0, \; \tau_1, \dots, \tau_{K-k+1} = 1.\]

The augmented knot sequence extends \(k\) knots beyond each boundary to handle the edges.

Start with order-1 (piecewise constant) bases:

\[B_{i,1}(z) = \mathbf{1}_{[\tau_i, \tau_{i+1})}(z).\]

Then recursively blend for orders \(m = 2, \dots, k+1\):

\[B_{i,m}(z) = \frac{z - \tau_i}{\tau_{i+m-1} - \tau_i} \, B_{i,m-1}(z) + \frac{\tau_{i+m} - z}{\tau_{i+m} - \tau_{i+1}} \, B_{i+1,m-1}(z).\]

Each blend raises the order by one and shrinks the basis count by one, so \(K\) functions of order \(k+1\) come out at the end. The result is an \(n \times K\) design matrix \(B\). Each row sums to 1 (the bricks tile the space) and each column has compact support (localised bumps).

Why cubic? linGAM defaults to spline_order=3, which the recursion above turns into basis functions of order \(k+1 = 4\) — cubic polynomials, degree 3. Cubic is the lowest degree that gives continuous second derivatives — the curve looks smooth to the human eye. Lower orders look jagged; higher orders increase computation without visible benefit.

Linear extrapolation. Outside \([0,1]\), B-splines can oscillate or collapse to zero — not useful for prediction beyond the training range. linGAM replaces the B-spline values with a linear extension using the boundary derivative:

\[f(z) \approx f(0) + f'(0) \, z \quad (z < 0), \qquad f(z) \approx f(1) + f'(1) \, (z-1) \quad (z > 1).\]

The derivative \(f'(0)\) is computed analytically from the order-\(k\) bases saved during the last step of the recursion, using the standard B-spline derivative formula \(B'_{i,k+1} = k \bigl( B_{i,k}/\Delta\tau - B_{i+1,k}/\Delta\tau \bigr)\).

Periodic basis. When constraint='periodic', the domain wraps around: the input is taken modulo 1 and the first \(k-1\) columns fold into the last \(k-1\), enforcing \(f(0) = f(1)\) and reducing the coefficient count from \(K\) to \(K_{\text{eff}} = K - k + 1\).

Penalties: why flexibility needs a cost¶

Suppose we give the model \(K = 30\) basis functions. It could fit the data almost perfectly — including every random noise wiggle. When we then predict on new data, the model falls apart. This is overfitting.

The solution is to penalise complexity. We don’t forbid wiggles; we charge a tax for them. The model can still wiggle, but only if doing so improves the fit enough to be worth the tax.

The penalised least-squares objective is:

\[\underbrace{\|\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2}_{\text{fit to data}} \;+\; \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top P \boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{complexity penalty}}.\]

The first term rewards fitting the training data closely. The second term punishes certain patterns in the coefficients. The smoothing parameter \(\lambda\) (lam in the API) controls the tax rate:

  • \(\lambda = 0\): no penalty — the curve can be as wiggly as the basis allows. Equivalent to unpenalised regression.

  • \(\lambda \to \infty\): infinite penalty — the curve is forced to be as smooth as possible (a straight line for second-difference penalties).

  • \(0 < \lambda < \infty\): a balance. linGAM uses grid search to find the \(\lambda\) that minimises GCV.

What each penalty does to the curve:

Second-difference penalty (default): Penalises the curvature (second derivative) of \(f(x)\). A straight line has zero curvature, so it costs nothing. Wiggles cost a lot. This produces the visually “smooth” curves we expect.

\[\begin{split}D_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 1 & & \\ & 1 & -2 & 1 & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots \end{pmatrix}_{(K-2) \times K}, \qquad P = \lambda \, D_2^\top D_2.\end{split}\]

First-difference penalty (monotonicity): Penalises changes between adjacent coefficients. If all adjacent coefficients are similar, the curve can’t reverse direction — hence the curve is pushed toward being monotonic.

\[\begin{split}D_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & & \\ & -1 & 1 & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots \end{pmatrix}_{(K-1) \times K}, \qquad P = \lambda \, D_1^\top D_1.\end{split}\]

Circular second-difference (periodicity): The second-difference operator wraps around, connecting the last coefficient back to the first — the mathematical equivalent of gluing the two ends of the curve together.

Ridge penalty: For factor terms (and linear terms, if penalised), \(P = \lambda I_K\). This is a “shrink-toward-zero” penalty — it pulls all coefficients toward zero by the same amount. (Linear l() terms default to \(\lambda = 0\): unpenalised.)

A honest caveat about “constraints”. The constraint= argument maps mono_inc/mono_dec to the first-difference penalty and convex/concave to the second-difference penalty. These are soft pushes, not hard constraints: a heavily penalised first-difference fit is almost monotonic but is never forced to be exactly monotonic. For hard guarantees you would need an inequality-constrained solver — a different mathematical problem altogether (and one reason the mgcv backend does not offer these options at all).

The role of \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) cannot be overstated. \(\lambda\) determines how much information the model extracts from the data vs. how much it imposes from the smoothness prior. Too small → overfitting (the model chases noise). Too large → underfitting (the model misses real patterns). Grid search finds the Goldilocks value automatically.

The SVD data-augmentation solver¶

Once we have the design matrix \(X\) and the penalty \(P\), we need to find the coefficients \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) that minimise the penalised objective.

The naive approach forms the normal equations:

\[(X^\top X + P)\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = X^\top \mathbf{y}.\]

This is mathematically correct but numerically dangerous. Forming \(X^\top X\) squares the condition number — if \(X\) has a condition number of \(10^4\), then \(X^\top X\) has \(10^8\). On a computer with 16-digit precision, this leaves very little room for error.

The data-augmentation trick treats the penalty as “fake data”:

\[\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} X \\ E \end{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\beta} \approx \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{y} \\ \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix},\end{split}\]

where \(E\) satisfies \(E^\top E = P + \varepsilon I\) (a tiny ridge \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(P\) is positive definite even when \(\lambda = 0\); in the code \(E\) is the transposed Cholesky factor of \(P + \varepsilon I\)). The top block says “fit the actual data.” The bottom block says “keep the coefficients small in the penalised directions.”

Solving this augmented system is equivalent to the penalised normal equations, but never forms \(X^\top X\). Instead, linGAM uses:

  1. QR decomposition of \(X = QR\). \(R\) is small (\(m \times m\), where \(m = \sum K_j + 1\)), so subsequent operations are cheap even when \(n\) is huge.

  2. SVD of the stacked matrix \([R; E] = U \Sigma V^\top\). The singular value decomposition is the most numerically stable way to factor a matrix — it exposes the “directions” in which the data has information and the directions it doesn’t.

  3. Solution operator \(B_{\text{solve}} = V \Sigma^{-1} U_1^\top Q^\top\) so that \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = B_{\text{solve}} \mathbf{y}\). This is saved and reused for covariance, EDF, and confidence intervals — no re-solving needed. (\(U_1\) is the top \(m \times m\) block of \(U\), the part corresponding to the data block \(R\).)

The SVD approach is especially important when \(\lambda\) is very small (the near-unpenalised case) or very large (near-zero coefficients), where the normal equations become ill-conditioned. By working with the square-root of \(X^\top X + P\) rather than the matrix itself, the SVD solver stays accurate across the entire range of \(\lambda\).

Effective Degrees of Freedom (EDF)¶

In ordinary linear regression with \(p\) predictors, the model uses exactly \(p\) degrees of freedom — one per coefficient. You can think of each degree of freedom as the model’s ability to “move” in one independent direction to fit the data.

Penalised splines blur this picture. The model has \(K\) coefficients (basis functions), but the penalty restricts how freely each one can move. A heavily penalised coefficient is “shrunken” toward its neighbours — it costs you an entire degree of freedom to include, but the penalty means you only use a fraction of it.

The EDF measures how many independent directions the fitted model actually explores. It is always between 0 and \(K\), and usually much closer to the number of “real features” in the data.

Mathematically, the EDF is the trace of the influence (hat) matrix:

\[\text{EDF} = \operatorname{tr}(H), \qquad H = X (X^\top X + P)^{-1} X^\top.\]

Using the SVD augmentation from the solver, this simplifies to:

\[\text{EDF} = \sum_{i} \sigma_i(U_1)^2 = \|U_1\|_F^2,\]

where \(U_1\) is the data block of the SVD’s left singular vectors. Why the equality holds: with \(X = QR\) and \([R;E] = U\Sigma V^\top\), the hat matrix factors as \(H = Q U_1 U_1^\top Q^\top\), so its trace is \(\operatorname{tr}(U_1^\top Q^\top Q U_1) = \|U_1\|_F^2\). This is computed in a single NumPy call with no matrix inversion.

What EDF tells you in practice:

  • EDF ≈ 2: the term is essentially a straight line (2 df = intercept + slope).

  • EDF ≈ K: the penalty is very weak; the term is using nearly all its basis functions.

  • EDF << K with good fit: the penalty is working well — the data has a smooth trend that the model captures with few effective parameters.

  • EDF growing while GCV stays flat: you’re overfitting — the extra wiggle doesn’t help prediction.

Per-coefficient EDF tells you which basis functions are doing the work:

\[\text{EDF}_j = \sum_i U_{1,ij}^2.\]

A coefficient with EDF \(\approx 0\) is essentially ignored by the model — its basis function could be removed without consequence.

Generalised Cross Validation (GCV)¶

The problem. How do we know if our model is good? We could hold out some data, fit on the rest, and check how well it predicts the held-out points. But we’d have to do this many times (cross-validation), which is slow — especially during grid search where we evaluate thousands of models.

The clever solution. Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) fits the model \(n\) times, each time dropping one data point and predicting it. This is \(O(n)\) fits, prohibitive for anything but tiny datasets.

GCV is a closed-form approximation of LOOCV that requires only one fit. The formula:

\[\text{GCV} = \frac{n \cdot \text{RSS}} {(n - \gamma \cdot \text{EDF})^2}.\]

Let’s unpack each piece:

  • \(n\): number of observations — a larger dataset gives a more stable estimate.

  • \(\text{RSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\): how far the predictions are from the actual values. Lower is better (better fit).

  • \(\text{EDF}\): effective degrees of freedom — the model’s complexity. More EDF means the model can “chase” data points more aggressively.

  • \(\gamma\): the GCV penalty multiplier (default 1.4 in the pygam backend). Setting \(\gamma > 1\) makes the criterion slightly conservative — it prefers simpler models, analogous to AIC’s penalty term.

The denominator \((n - \gamma \cdot \text{EDF})^2\) is the key. When EDF is small (simple model), the denominator is large → GCV is small → good. When EDF grows, the denominator shrinks → GCV explodes → bad, unless the extra complexity reduces RSS enough to compensate.

Why GCV and not plain CV? GCV is asymptotically equivalent to LOOCV but computes in \(O(1)\) extra time after a single fit. It’s the reason linGAM’s grid search can evaluate thousands of hyperparameter combinations in seconds rather than minutes.

Interpreting GCV values:

  • GCV is in squared units of \(y\). Comparing GCV between models on the same dataset tells you which is better; comparing across datasets does not.

  • A GCV that drops dramatically when you add a term means the term is useful.

  • A GCV that stays flat or increases when you add a term means the term is unnecessary noise.

  • The absolute value matters less than the relative value across models.

Putting it together: the penalised fit¶

Let’s trace what happens when you call model.fit(x, y) with the pygam backend:

  1. Parse the formula. "s(0) + te(1,2) + f(3)" becomes a list of term objects, each knowing its feature column(s), basis count, and penalty type.

  2. Build design matrices. Each term constructs its B-spline basis (or one-hot encoding for factors, or just a column for linear terms). These are stacked side-by-side, plus an intercept column of ones, to form the full design matrix \(X\) (size \(n \times m\)).

  3. Build the penalty. Each term’s penalty matrix is computed and assembled into a block-diagonal \(P\) (size \(m \times m\)). The intercept block is zero — we never penalise the overall level.

  4. Solve. The SVD data-augmentation solver finds \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and stores the solution operator \(B_{\text{solve}}\) for later use.

  5. Compute diagnostics. RSS, EDF, GCV, scale estimate, covariance matrix, standard errors — all available via model.statistics_.

Why the intercept is special. If we penalised the intercept, the model would be forced toward \(y = 0\), which is almost never what we want. The intercept absorbs the overall level, letting the penalised terms focus on shape. This is why fit_intercept=True is the default and why the intercept block in \(P\) is zero.

A note on identifiability. The default second-difference penalty does not charge constant or linear trends (they lie in \(D_2\)’s null space). Together with the unpenalised intercept, this pins down the decomposition: the intercept owns the level, and each smooth owns only its bending. The pygam backend relies on this implicit mechanism. The mgcv backend, as we’ll see, makes the centering explicit with a sum-to-zero constraint — same goal, different route.

Tensor-product interactions¶

An additive model with only univariate terms cannot capture relationships where the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another. For example, high temperature might be especially damaging at high vibration — this is a synergistic interaction.

The tensor product te(f1, f2, ..., fd) models this by building a multi-dimensional smooth surface. The design matrix is the column-wise Kronecker product of marginal B-spline bases:

\[B_{\text{tensor}} = B_1 \odot B_2 \odot \dots \odot B_d.\]

If \(B_1\) is \(n \times K_1\) and \(B_2\) is \(n \times K_2\), then \(B_{\text{tensor}}\) is \(n \times (K_1 K_2)\). This grows quickly — a 2-D tensor with \(K_1 = K_2 = 6\) creates 36 columns; with \(K_1 = K_2 = 10\) it’s 100 columns. This is why tensor terms use smaller default \(K\) values (4-8) than univariate splines (5-25).

The penalty is a Kronecker sum — each dimension gets its own smoothing parameter:

\[P_{\text{tensor}} = \sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d \, \bigl( I_{K_1} \otimes \dots \otimes P_d \otimes \dots \otimes I_{K_D} \bigr).\]

This means smoothness is enforced independently in each direction. A surface can be smooth in temperature but wiggly in vibration, or vice versa. (Pass a list to lam= to give each dimension its own \(\lambda_d\); a scalar is broadcast to all dimensions.)

When to use a tensor vs. separate s() terms. If the interaction exists, a model with only s(temperature) + s(vibration) will show patterned residuals — the error at high-temp-high-vibration will be systematically wrong. Adding te(temperature, vibration) captures this extra structure. Check the decomposition plot: if the te() heatmap shows a strong diagonal pattern, the interaction is real.

Confidence and prediction intervals¶

A point prediction says “the model thinks blade life is 42.3 cycles.” An interval says “the model thinks blade life is between 40.1 and 44.5 cycles, with 95% confidence.” Intervals quantify uncertainty.

Confidence intervals answer: How precisely do we know the average response at this point? They capture uncertainty in the coefficient estimates. Narrow where we have lots of data; wide where data is sparse.

Prediction intervals answer: Where would a single new observation likely fall? They add the residual variability \(\hat\sigma^2\) to the confidence interval width. A prediction interval is always wider than a confidence interval at the same point — individual observations are noisier than averages.

The formulas:

\[\text{Var}(\hat y(\mathbf{x}^*)) = \mathbf{x}^{*\top} \, \text{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \, \mathbf{x}^*,\]
\[\text{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = B_{\text{solve}} B_{\text{solve}}^\top \, \hat\sigma^2, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - \text{EDF}}.\]

Confidence intervals:

\[\hat y(\mathbf{x}^*) \pm t_{\alpha/2, \, n-\text{EDF}} \, \sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat y(\mathbf{x}^*))}.\]

Prediction intervals:

\[\hat y(\mathbf{x}^*) \pm t_{\alpha/2, \, n-\text{EDF}} \, \sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat y(\mathbf{x}^*)) + \hat\sigma^2}.\]

We use the t-distribution (not the normal) because \(\sigma\) is estimated from the data. Degrees of freedom are \(n - \text{EDF}\) because the penalty has already “used up” EDF worth of information.

This covariance is the frequentist one — it treats \(\lambda\) as fixed and propagates only the sampling variability of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). The mgcv backend additionally computes a Bayesian covariance (treating the penalty as a prior); the difference is explained in Part III.

Fast grid search: how it works¶

Grid search evaluates every combination of \(K\) (n_splines) and \(\lambda\) (lam) candidates. A naïve implementation would rebuild \(X\) and solve from scratch for each combination — prohibitively slow.

linGAM’s fast path splits the work into two phases:

Phase 1 — Precompute per \(\boldsymbol{K}\) (threaded). For each candidate basis count \(K\):

  1. Build \(X_K\) and compute \(X_K = Q_K R_K\) (QR).

  2. Cache \(R_K^\top R_K\) and \(R_K^\top Q_K^\top \mathbf{y}\). These are independent of \(\lambda\).

  3. Precompute the unscaled penalty basis \(S = D^\top D\) at \(\lambda = 1\).

All \(K\)-configurations are processed in parallel when n_jobs != 1 (ThreadPoolExecutor; NumPy releases the GIL during QR decomposition, so CPU-bound linear algebra genuinely runs on multiple cores). With the default n_jobs=1 everything runs serially.

Phase 2 — Evaluate per \(\boldsymbol{(K, \lambda)}\) (threaded). For each combination:

  1. Assemble penalty: \(P = \lambda S\).

  2. Form \(B = R_K^\top R_K + P\).

  3. Cholesky solve for \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and EDF.

  4. Compute RSS and GCV.

Cholesky costs \(O(m^3/3)\) vs. \(O(m^3)\) for SVD, and it’s numerically safe because \(R_K^\top R_K + P\) is positive definite (the penalty adds ridge stabilisation). Both the K-precomputation and the per-K evaluation loop use the same n_jobs-gated threading.

Why this matters. For a model with \(m = 20\) coefficients, \(n = 500\) observations, and a grid of \(8 \times 8 = 64\) combinations: a naïve sweep takes ~64 SVDs of \(500 \times 20\) matrices. The fast path does ~8 QR decompositions (one per unique \(K\)) and ~64 Cholesky solves (one per \((K, \lambda)\) pair), which is roughly 10× faster. The gap widens with larger \(n\).

Each smooth term (and each tensor dimension) owns its own \(\lambda\) slot in the grid, so the search optimises a vector of smoothing parameters jointly. A scalar lam= grid is broadcast to every slot when you want the classic “one \(\lambda\) for the whole model” behaviour.

Huber IRLS: handling outliers¶

Real data has outliers — sensor glitches, data-entry errors, anomalous operating conditions. Ordinary least squares weights every point equally, so a single extreme outlier can pull the entire curve toward it.

The Huber loss replaces squared error with a hybrid: small residuals are penalised quadratically (like OLS), large residuals are penalised linearly (less harshly). The transition point \(c\) is set automatically from the data’s median absolute deviation (MAD):

\[\begin{split}\rho(r) = \begin{cases} \tfrac12 r^2 & |r| \le c \\ c(|r| - \tfrac12 c) & |r| > c \end{cases}, \qquad c = 1.345 \cdot \text{MAD} / 0.6745.\end{split}\]

The constant 1.345 gives ~95% asymptotic efficiency under Gaussian errors — when there are no outliers, the robust fit is almost as good as OLS. When there are outliers, it’s vastly better.

IRLS iterates:

  1. Fit the model with current weights.

  2. Compute residuals \(r_i = y_i - \hat y_i\).

  3. Update weights: \(w_i = \min(1, \, c / |r_i|)\). Points with large residuals get small weights — they’re effectively ignored.

  4. Re-fit with the new weights. Repeat until convergence.

This is equivalent to M-estimation with the Huber ψ-function. linGAM implements it in irls_solve (used via fit(x, y, robust=True)) by scaling each row of \(X\) and element of \(\mathbf{y}\) by \(\sqrt{w_i}\) before calling the standard PIRLS solver, running up to 15 such re-weighting iterations. The reported RSS — and hence the scale estimate and GCV — use the final weights, \(\sum_i w_i r_i^2\), so outliers don’t inflate the reported uncertainty either.

When to use robust fitting:

  • You suspect outliers (always a good default in engineering data).

  • Your residuals show a few extreme values.

  • Standard and robust fits give very different GCV scores – the standard fit is being distorted by outliers.

When NOT to use it:

  • Your data is clean and you need maximum speed (robust is ~5x slower due to iterations).

  • Your “outliers” are actually the most important data points (e.g., rare failure events you want to model accurately).

This option is pygam-only; the mgcv backend currently fits by plain penalised least squares.

Part III — The mgcv backend¶

How the mgcv backend thinks¶

The mgcv backend (backend='mgcv') is a faithful Python port of Simon Wood’s R package mgcv (Wood 2006, 2017). Where the pygam backend bets on one basis and a grid search, mgcv bets on richness and automatic inference:

  1. A zoo of bases. Seven basis families ('tp', 'ts', 'cr', 'cs', 'cc', 'ps', 're' — plus 'cp') with different knot placements, different penalties, and different shrinkage behaviour. Each solves the smoothness problem a slightly different way.

  2. One smoothing parameter per penalty, estimated. Instead of sweeping a grid, the backend treats \(\lambda\) as a free parameter and optimises a model-selection criterion — Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) by default, GCV as an option — in log-\(\lambda\) space with standard optimisers.

  3. Explicit identifiability. Every smooth is centred by absorbing a sum-to-zero constraint into the basis itself, and every penalty is rescaled to a common scale (mgcv’s S.scale), so the \(\lambda\) values are comparable across terms.

  4. Full inferential machinery. Bayesian and frequentist covariances, per-term approximate F-tests with p-values (Wood 2013), AIC/BIC, deviance explained.

The pipeline is:

\[\text{formula} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{basis + penalty per term}}_{\S 1} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{rescale, centre}}_{\S 2} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{optimise } \lambda \text{ by REML/GCV}}_{\S 3} \;\to\; \underbrace{\text{inference}}_{\S 4}.\]

Sections 1–4 below follow that order.

The basis zoo¶

All of the mgcv bases share one objective: represent a smooth \(f(x)\) as a linear combination of basis functions with an attached wiggliness penalty \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S \boldsymbol{\beta}\). Three of the families (tp, cr, cc) penalise the exact curvature integral \(\int f''(x)^2\,dx\); the P-splines penalise a discrete difference approximation of it; the random effect family penalises the coefficients directly. Here’s the map:

The table’s “null space” column matters more than it looks: those are the function shapes that cost nothing to include. A penalty with a null space leaves the corresponding pattern unpenalised and lets the intercept (or the model’s other terms) absorb it.

Thin plate regression splines (tp, ts)¶

The default in mgcv, and the most mathematically interesting family. It starts from a continuous problem, not a knot placement.

The continuous problem. Among all functions with two derivatives, find the \(f\) minimising

\[\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl( y_i - f(x_i) \bigr)^2 + \lambda \int f''(x)^2 \, dx.\]

The first term is ordinary least squares; the second charges the total squared curvature. It turns out (the representer theorem for splines) that the minimiser has the form

\[f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i \, \eta(|x - x_i|) + \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x, \qquad \eta(r) = \frac{|r|^3}{12},\]

subject to \(\sum_i \delta_i = \sum_i \delta_i x_i = 0\) (the \(T^\top\delta = 0\) constraint). The \(n\) “radial” basis functions sit one on each data point; the two polynomial terms form the null space — they have zero curvature, so the penalty never touches them.

Why \(\boldsymbol{\eta(r) = |r|^3/12}\) ? It is the Green’s function of the fourth-derivative operator:

\[\frac{d^4}{dr^4}\left(\frac{|r|^3}{12}\right) = \delta(r),\]

where \(\delta\) is the Dirac delta. Consequence: for any function of the form above, the curvature integral collapses to a quadratic form in the coefficients,

\[\int f''(x)^2 \, dx \;=\; \boldsymbol{\delta}^\top E \boldsymbol{\delta}, \qquad E_{ij} = \eta(|x_i - x_j|).\]

A one-line sanity check: for \(r > 0\), \(\eta'''(r) = 1/2\) (and \(-1/2\) for \(r < 0\)), so the third derivative jumps by exactly 1 at the origin — which is what makes the fourth derivative a unit Dirac spike. The “thin plate” name comes from the \(d=2\) generalisation, where the penalty is the bending energy of a physical plate.

Conditional positive definiteness. The matrix \(E\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues, but it is positive definite on the subspace orthogonal to the null space (\(T^\top\delta = 0\)). Solving the continuous problem exactly gives \(f\) with one parameter per data point (an \(O(n)\) model) — beautiful, but too expensive and over-flexible for practical use.

The low-rank approximation. mgcv’s trick (and linGAM’s) is to keep only the \(k\) most important radial directions. Eigen-decompose

\[E = U \operatorname{diag}(v) U^\top,\]

sort eigenpairs by \(|v_j|\), and truncate to the top \(k\):

\[E_k = U_k \operatorname{diag}(v_k) U_k^\top.\]

(The code uses ARPACK’s eigsh for speed when there are many unique points, and falls back to a full eigh otherwise.) The retained eigenfunctions are the smoothest, largest-scale modes — exactly the structure you want in a smooth — while the discarded high-frequency modes are the ones a penalty would crush anyway.

Absorbing the constraint. We still need the retained directions to be orthogonal to the null space, i.e. \(T^\top U_k \delta = 0\). Compute a Householder rotation \(Q\) such that

\[T^\top U_k \, Q = \bigl[\,0_{M \times (k-M)} \;\; R\,\bigr], \qquad M = 2.\]

Then the first \(k-M\) columns of \(U_k Q\) span exactly the retained modes that are orthogonal to constants and linear terms. The basis and penalty become

\[X = \Bigl[\, U_k \operatorname{diag}(v_k) Q_{[:, :k-M]} \;\;\; T \,\Bigr], \qquad S = Q^\top \operatorname{diag}(v_k) Q \;\text{with rows/cols}\; k-M \dots k-1 \;\text{zeroed}.\]

The last \(M\) columns of \(X\) are \([1, x-\bar x]\) (the null space, unpenalised); the first \(k-M\) columns are the penalised modes, each charged by its eigenvalue \(v_j\).

Column rescaling. Finally each column of \(X\) is scaled to unit root-mean-square and \(S\) is divided by the corresponding row/column products (\(S_{ij} \leftarrow S_{ij} / (w_i w_j)\)). This keeps the numerical scale of \(X\) and \(S\) comparable no matter what units \(x\) is measured in.

Prediction at new points follows the same construction without re-truncating: \(X_{\text{new}} = \bigl[ E_{\text{new}} U_k Q_{[:, :k-M]},\;\; [1, x_{\text{new}} - \bar x] \bigr]\) (then divided by the same column scales), where \((E_{\text{new}})_{ij} = \eta(|x_i^{\text{new}} - x_j^{\text{train}}|)\).

Shrinkage (``ts``). The penalty \(S\) above has a two-dimensional null space (the \(T\) part). That means \(\lambda\) can shrink the wiggly part all it wants, but the linear trend in \(f\) is never penalised — a tp smooth can never be removed from the model. The ts variant changes this by eigen-decomposing \(S\) and giving the null-space eigenvalues a small positive value:

\[\text{ev}_{0}, \text{ev}_{1} \leftarrow \text{ev}_2 \times 0.1,\]

which charges the linear trend just enough that a strong \(\lambda\) can shrink the whole smooth to zero. (This is also how model selection can effectively drop a term.)

Cubic regression splines (cr, cs)¶

If thin plate splines are the elegant continuous solution, cubic regression splines are the workhorse discrete one. The idea: place \(k\) knots at the sample quantiles of the unique \(x\) values, demand that \(f\) be a cubic polynomial between knots, twice continuously differentiable at each knot, and linear outside the range of the knots (the “natural” boundary condition: \(f'' = 0\) beyond the first and last knot).

The value–curvature parametrisation. A natural cubic spline is fully determined by its values at the knots together with the natural boundary condition. Within an interval \([x_j, x_{j+1}]\) of width \(h_j\), the spline interpolates between knot values \(f_j, f_{j+1}\) and second derivatives \(\gamma_j, \gamma_{j+1}\):

\[f(x) = \frac{(x_{j+1}-x)^3 - h_j^2(x_{j+1}-x)}{6h_j}\,\gamma_j + \frac{(x-x_j)^3 - h_j^2(x-x_j)}{6h_j}\,\gamma_{j+1} + \frac{x_{j+1}-x}{h_j}\, f_j + \frac{x-x_j}{h_j}\, f_{j+1}.\]

(This is the formula the _eval_cr_basis code implements, with \(\gamma = F\boldsymbol{\beta}\) and the linear hat functions added on top.)

Two linear systems connect everything. For \(n_k\) knots:

  • The second derivatives at the knots are a linear function of the knot values, \(\boldsymbol{\gamma} = B^{-1} D \,\mathbf{f}\), where \(D\) is the \((n_k-2) \times n_k\) divided-second-difference matrix

    \[\begin{split}D = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{h_1} & -(\frac{1}{h_1}+\frac{1}{h_2}) & \frac{1}{h_2} & & \\ & \frac{1}{h_2} & -(\frac{1}{h_2}+\frac{1}{h_3}) & \frac{1}{h_3} & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots \end{pmatrix},\end{split}\]

    and \(B\) is the symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal \((h_j + h_{j+1})/3\) and off-diagonal \(h_{j+1}/6\).

  • The curvature integral then factorises as

    \[\int f''(x)^2\,dx \;=\; \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top B \boldsymbol{\gamma} \;=\; \mathbf{f}^\top D^\top B^{-1} D \,\mathbf{f} \;\Rightarrow\; S = D^\top B^{-1} D.\]

    Deriving it is a two-line calculus exercise: between knots \(f''\) is a straight line, so its integral is exactly the quadratic form with the tridiagonal \(B\).

\(S\) has rank \(k-2\): its null space is the two-dimensional space of linear functions (straight lines have no curvature), which again remain unpenalised. Extrapolation beyond the boundary knots is linear by construction — the natural boundary condition is linear extrapolation, so cr behaves predictably outside the data range.

Shrinkage (``cs``) is the discrete twin of ts: eigen-decompose \(S\), and charge the two null-space eigenvalues at 0.1× and 0.01× the smallest positive one:

\[\text{ev}_1 \leftarrow \text{ev}_2 \times 0.1, \qquad \text{ev}_0 \leftarrow \text{ev}_1 \times 0.1.\]

The linear trend is now weakly penalised, so a strong \(\lambda\) can shrink the whole term toward zero.

Cyclic cubic regression splines (cc)¶

For quantities on a circle — time-of-day, wind direction, phase angles — the boundary values should agree: \(f(x_0) = f(x_1)\) and matching derivatives. The cyclic cubic spline (Lancaster & Salkauskas 1986) takes the cr construction and wraps it: knots are placed evenly through the sorted unique \(x\) values, and the \(B\) and \(D\) matrices become circulant — the last interval connects back to the first, as in the code’s build_cc_basis:

\[B_{0,0} = \frac{h_{n-1} + h_0}{3}, \quad B_{0,1} = \frac{h_0}{6}, \quad B_{0,n-1} = \frac{h_{n-1}}{6},\]

with the mirror entries on the last row, and similarly for \(D\). The penalty is the same form, \(S = D^\top B^{-1} D\), now of rank \(k-2\) with a one-dimensional null space — constants only, since a periodic function that is “straight” is exactly constant. Evaluating the basis wraps the covariate cyclically onto \([x_0, x_1]\) first.

P-splines (ps, cp)¶

Eilers & Marx (1996) cut the problem even further: forget exact curvature integrals; place a uniformly spaced grid of knots (extended 0.1% beyond the data range, plus \(m_{\text{basis}}+1\) knots past each end so all \(k\) basis functions are well defined), build cubic B-splines on it, and penalise the :math:`m`-th order differences of adjacent coefficients:

\[S = D^\top D, \qquad D = \underbrace{\Delta^m}_{\text{repeated differencing}}, \qquad (k-m) \times k.\]

The default is \(m = 2\): second differences, the discrete counterpart of curvature. The penalty’s null space is the space of polynomials of degree \(< m\) — for \(m=2\), linear trends are free. P-splines trade a little elegance for speed and simplicity (the penalty needs no matrix inverse, unlike \(B^{-1}\) in cr), and the equal knot spacing makes the basis numerically well behaved.

For cyclic P-splines ('cp'), both the B-spline basis (via mgcv’s cSplineDes knot wrapping) and the \(m\)-th order difference penalty wrap around the boundaries, leaving only constants in the one-dimensional null space.

Random-effect smooths (re)¶

For a categorical predictor with many levels, re builds one column per level (an identity/one-hot design matrix) and penalises the coefficients with \(S = I\) — pure ridge shrinkage:

\[\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S \boldsymbol{\beta} = \sum_j \beta_j^2.\]

In the Bayesian view (see the REML section) this is exactly a random-effects model: level effects drawn from \(N(0, \sigma^2 / \lambda)\), and \(\lambda\) estimated from the data is the inverse-variance of the random effect. Larger \(\lambda\) shrinks all level effects toward zero, pooling the levels together.

Identifiability: rescaling and the sum-to-zero constraint¶

A GAM with an intercept is over-parametrised: adding a constant to a smooth \(f_j\) and subtracting it from the intercept leaves every prediction unchanged. Fitting “works” regardless, but the decomposition becomes arbitrary — you cannot say whether the average blade life came from the intercept or from the temperature term. mgcv resolves this with two standard moves, both applied to every smooth term before fitting.

Move 1 — ``S.scale``: rescale each penalty. A penalty’s raw size depends on its basis: a basis of large-magnitude functions produces a large \(S\). To make the smoothing parameter mean “amount of smoothing” rather than “basis scale × amount of smoothing”, each penalty is normalised by

\[\text{S.scale}_i = \frac{\|S_i\|_{\text{O}}}{\|X\|_{\text{I}}^2}, \qquad S_i \leftarrow \frac{S_i}{\text{S.scale}_i},\]

where \(\|\cdot\|_{\text{O}}\) is the maximum column sum (the operator norm of a symmetric matrix) and \(\|\cdot\|_{\text{I}}\) is the maximum row sum of \(X\), squared. The scale is saved, so reported \(\lambda\) values are on this normalised scale — comparable across terms and across basis families.

Move 2 — ``absorb.cons``: absorb the sum-to-zero constraint. The constraint is that each smooth’s fitted values average to zero:

\[C \boldsymbol{\beta} = 0, \qquad C = \mathbf{1}^\top X \;\; \text{(the row of column sums)}.\]

Rather than solving a constrained problem, the constraint is absorbed into the basis: compute the full QR of \(C^\top\) (\(k \times 1\)), take \(Z = Q_{[:, 1:]}\) — an orthonormal basis of \(\ker C\) — and project:

\[\tilde X = X Z, \qquad \tilde S_i = Z^\top S_i Z.\]

Now \(\mathbf{1}^\top \tilde X = 0\) identically: the smooth is centred by construction, in every fit, at every \(\lambda\), and in every prediction. The intercept owns the level; each smooth owns only its shape. This is why mgcv decomposition panels are genuinely centred at zero, while the pygam panels rely on the intercept to absorb levels.

For tensor-product terms the same pipeline applies after assembling the Kronecker-sum penalties; each marginal penalty is first normalised by its largest eigenvalue (so the dimensions contribute to the penalty on equal footing), then the usual S.scale + absorb.cons pass runs on the full tensor basis.

Smoothing parameter selection: REML and GCV.Cp¶

Both backends minimise the same penalised objective,

\[\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta} \|^2 + \sum_i \lambda_i \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S_i \boldsymbol{\beta} = \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta} \|^2 + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} \boldsymbol{\beta},\]

but they choose \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) differently. The pygam backend sweeps a grid and scores each point with GCV. The mgcv backend treats \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) as continuous parameters of a model-selection criterion and optimises. For a fixed \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\), the fit is obtained by QR of \(X\) and a Cholesky solve of

\[H = R^\top R + S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} = L L^\top, \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = H^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}.\]

(With the tiny ridge on \(H\)’s diagonal guarding the \(\lambda = 0\) edge case.)

GCV.Cp. The same criterion as the pygam backend, computed from the Cholesky factor instead of an SVD. The EDF is

\[\text{EDF} = \operatorname{tr}(H^{-1} R^\top R) = \| L^{-1} R^\top \|_F^2,\]

(a trace identity: \(\operatorname{tr}(ABA^\top) = \|AB^{1/2}\|_F^2\) with \(A = R\), \(B = H^{-1} = L^{-\top}L^{-1}\)), and the score is

\[V_g(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \frac{n \cdot \text{RSS}}{(n - \gamma \cdot \text{EDF})^2}, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - \text{EDF}}.\]

Here the default \(\gamma = 1\) (mgcv’s GCV.Cp), versus 1.4 in the pygam backend — a small but real difference between the two engines’ model-selection tastes.

REML (the default). Give the coefficients a Gaussian prior whose precision is the penalty,

\[\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, \quad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I), \qquad \boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N\bigl(0, \,\sigma^2 S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{-}\bigr),\]

where \(S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{-}\) denotes the (generalised) inverse — an improper prior that treats the penalty’s null space as infinite variance. Integrating \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) out gives the marginal (restricted) likelihood for \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) and \(\sigma^2\). Profiling out \(\sigma^2\) at

\[\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{D_p}{n - M_p}, \qquad D_p = \underbrace{\|\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|^2}_{\text{RSS}} + \underbrace{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\text{penalty cost}},\]

where \(M_p\) is the dimension of the parametric part of the model (the intercept, \(M_p = 1\)), the criterion to minimise is

\[\ell_r(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) \;=\; \frac{D_p}{2\hat\sigma^2} + \frac{n - M_p}{2} \log(2\pi\hat\sigma^2) + \frac12 \log |H| - \frac12 \log |S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|_+.\]

Reading it term by term:

  • \(D_p / 2\hat\sigma^2\): how well the penalised fit explains the data, measured against the estimated noise. The first two terms together are \((n-M_p)(1 + \log 2\pi\hat\sigma^2)/2\) after substituting \(\hat\sigma^2\) — a pure function of the penalised deviance.

  • \(\frac12 \log|H|\): a complexity tax. The more the penalty is weakened, the larger \(H\)’s determinant, the worse the score. This term is what prevents \(\lambda \to 0\).

  • \(-\frac12 \log|S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|_+\): a normalisation correction for the prior. \(|S|_+\) is the product of the positive eigenvalues only (the penalty is singular by design — its null space would otherwise contribute \(\log 0 = -\infty\)).

Why the “\(_+\)” matters can be seen by taking \(S_\lambda = \lambda S\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(S) = r\): \(\log|S_\lambda|_+ = r\log\lambda + \log|S|_+\), which scales correctly with the rank. The implementation computes it by eigendecomposition, summing logs of the strictly positive eigenvalues; when the penalties of different terms act on disjoint blocks of coefficients, it uses the factorisation

\[\log |S_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|_+ = \sum_i \Bigl[ \operatorname{rank}(S_i) \log \lambda_i + \sum_j \log \text{ev}^+_j(S_i) \Bigr],\]

and falls back to the general eigendecomposition otherwise (e.g. tensor terms, whose per-dimension penalties share the same coefficient block).

\(\log|H|\) needs no eigendecomposition: from the Cholesky factor, \(\log|H| = 2\sum_i \log L_{ii}\).

Why REML and not maximum likelihood? In the mixed-model view, estimating \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) costs degrees of freedom; plain ML ignores this and biases \(\sigma^2\) (and thus \(\lambda\)) downward — it under-smoothes. The restricted likelihood corrects for exactly this loss, which is why the criterion uses \(n - M_p\) instead of \(n\). REML also has better-behaved optima than GCV, which is notorious for flat minima and occasional near-zero \(\lambda\) solutions.

Optimising in log space. \(\lambda\) must be positive, so the backend optimises \(\rho = \log\lambda\) (unconstrained, with \(\lambda = e^\rho\)) over the range \(\rho \in [-15, 15]\) — i.e. \(\lambda\) between roughly \(3\times10^{-7}\) and \(3\times10^{6}\). One free \(\lambda\): Brent’s method (minimise_scalar, bounded) on the 1-D criterion. Several free \(\lambda\) (e.g. one per tensor dimension): L-BFGS-B starting from \(\rho = 0\) (\(\lambda = 1\)). Either way the fit is re-evaluated a handful of times — each evaluation one Cholesky — rather than at every point of a grid. Individual \(\lambda\) values can be pinned with sp= if you want some terms fixed and others estimated.

The REML score itself is reported in statistics_ along with the estimated \(\lambda\) values, so you can compare models on the restricted likelihood exactly as R users do.

Inference: two covariances, one F-test¶

With \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) estimated, the backend computes a full inferential kit. Two covariance matrices appear:

\[V_p = H^{-1}\hat\sigma^2, \qquad V_e = H^{-1} X^\top X H^{-1} \hat\sigma^2 = H^{-1} R^\top R H^{-1} \hat\sigma^2.\]

  • \(V_p\) is the Bayesian posterior covariance — the posterior of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) under the prior that generated REML, with \(\lambda\) treated as known. It is what mgcv reports in summary() tables and uses for confidence bands; standard errors are \(\operatorname{SE}_j = \sqrt{(V_p)_{jj}}\).

  • \(V_e\) is the frequentist (sandwich) covariance — the sampling covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) treating the penalty as part of the estimator, again with \(\lambda\) fixed. It ignores the uncertainty in \(\lambda\) itself (a standard simplification in the mgcv world, though the literature notes it makes intervals slightly optimistic).

Interval widths for a new point \(\mathbf{x}^*\) come from \(\mathbf{x}^{*\top} V_p \,\mathbf{x}^*\), with \(\hat\sigma^2\) added for prediction intervals; the implementation uses t quantiles with \(n - \text{EDF}\) degrees of freedom.

Per-coefficient and per-term EDF. From the influence matrix

\[F = H^{-1} R^\top R, \qquad \text{EDF} = \operatorname{tr}(F), \qquad \text{EDF}_j = F_{jj}.\]

Term-level EDF is the sum of \(F_{jj}\) over that term’s coefficient block. A term with EDF near 1 is essentially linear; a term whose EDF barely exceeds 1 despite a large \(k\) is doing very little.

Wood’s approximate F-tests. For each term, testing \(H_0:\; f_j = 0\) (in basis terms, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_j = 0\)), mgcv uses the test statistic (Wood 2013)

\[F_j = \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_j^\top V_{p,j}^{-1} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_j} {\text{EDF}_j} \;\sim\; F(\text{EDF}_j,\; n - \text{EDF}_{\text{total}}) \;\; \text{under } H_0,\]

with the p-value from the right tail of the F distribution. The justification is a moment-matching argument: under the null the quadratic form has mean \(\text{EDF}_j\) and variance \(2\,\text{EDF}_j\), matching an \(F\)-like distribution to second order. It is an approximation — exact for \(\lambda = 0\) (where it reduces to the classical F-test) and well-calibrated for EDF comfortably above 1, but p-values for terms with EDF barely above 1 should be read with suspicion (a known mgcv caveat).

Model-level summaries. The backend also reports:

\[\text{deviance explained} = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2}, \qquad R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}/(n-\text{EDF})} {\text{TSS}/(n-1)},\]

the Gaussian log-likelihood \(\ell = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\hat\sigma^2) - \tfrac{\text{RSS}}{2\hat\sigma^2}\), and the information criteria \(\text{AIC} = -2\ell + 2(\text{EDF}+1)\), \(\text{BIC} = -2\ell + \log(n)(\text{EDF}+1)\) — the \(+1\) counting the estimated \(\sigma^2\). These make the mgcv backend the choice when you need p-values, AIC-based model comparison, or output that matches an R summary.gam table.

Part IV — Backends compared¶

PyGAM vs mgcv: the explicit comparison¶

Both engines fit the same model to the same data with the same penalised objective. Everything else is a strategy choice. The table summarises the differences; the subsections after it explain the ones that matter.

Aspect

PyGAM backend

mgcv backend

Basis families

One: uniform B-spline, cubic default, linear extrapolation, periodic folding

Seven+: tp, ts, cr, cs, cc, ps, re (+ cp stub), mixable per tensor margin

Knot placement

Uniform over \([\min x, \max x]\)

Quantiles (cr/cs), even spread through unique values (cc), equally spaced (ps), knot-free eigen-basis (tp)

Smoothing parameters

One \(\lambda\) per term (per tensor dimension); grid can be broadcast to all

One \(\lambda\) per penalty matrix; each estimated independently

Selection method

Discrete grid search over \((K, \lambda)\), scored by GCV with \(\gamma = 1.4\)

Continuous optimisation of \(\log\lambda\); REML (default) or GCV.Cp with \(\gamma = 1\)

Solver

SVD data-augmentation of \([R; E]\) (never forms \(X^\top X\))

QR + Cholesky of \(R^\top R + S_\lambda\)

EDF computation

\(\|U_1\|_F^2\) from the augmented SVD

\(\operatorname{tr}(H^{-1}R^\top R) = \|L^{-1}R^\top\|_F^2\) from Cholesky

Identifiability

Implicit: unpenalised intercept + penalty null spaces

Explicit: S.scale rescaling + absorbed sum-to-zero constraint

Covariance

Frequentist \(B_{\text{solve}} B_{\text{solve}}^\top \hat\sigma^2\)

Bayesian \(V_p = H^{-1}\hat\sigma^2\) and frequentist \(V_e = H^{-1}R^\top R H^{-1}\hat\sigma^2\)

Intervals

t-based CI/PI, df \(= n - \text{EDF}\)

t-based on \(V_p\) (plus \(\hat\sigma^2\) for PI), df \(= n - \text{EDF}\)

Term significance

None — compare GCV scores between models

Wood (2013) approximate F-tests with p-values

Model metrics

GCV

REML/GCV score, AIC, BIC, deviance explained, adjusted \(R^2\)

Shape constraints

Soft: mono inc/dec, convex, concave via \(D_1\)/\(D_2\) penalties; periodic via wrapped basis

Periodic via cc (cp pending); no monotonic/convex options

Robust fitting

Huber IRLS, MAD-scaled

Not available (plain penalised least squares)

Cost profile

Many cheap evaluations (grid); threaded with n_jobs != 1; QR cached per \(K\)

Few, heavier evaluations (optimiser iterations); one QR, repeated Cholesky

Best fit for

Fast sweeps, shape constraints, outlier-heavy data, teaching the machinery

p-values & R parity, automatic \(\lambda\), basis choice, tensor margin mixing

The same objective, two strategies. Both engines minimise \(\|\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top S_\lambda \boldsymbol{\beta}\). The difference is only which \(\lambda\) you evaluate. Grid search is deterministic, embarrassingly parallel, and gives you the whole GCV surface to inspect — but its resolution is limited to the grid, and cost grows multiplicatively with the number of terms (each term adds a dimension to the grid). Optimisation is adaptive (it spends evaluations near the minimum), handles many \(\lambda\) values gracefully, and lands on the continuous optimum — but it converges to local minima, and REML’s surface is usually (though not always) nicer than GCV’s.

Numerics. The SVD solver is the more robust of the two across the full \(\lambda\) range — it never squares a condition number and it degrades gracefully at \(\lambda \to 0\). The Cholesky path is faster per solve (\(m^3/3\) vs \(\sim m^3\)) and is protected by the penalty itself, which keeps \(R^\top R + S_\lambda\) positive definite in practice. Both are exact up to floating point; on well-scaled data they agree to machine precision, and on ill-conditioned data the SVD path is the safer bet.

Inference. This is where the backends diverge most for the user. The pygam backend reports GCV and (t-based, frequentist) intervals and stops there — model selection is by comparing GCV between fits. The mgcv backend adds a Bayesian covariance, per-term p-values, AIC/BIC and an R-style summary. If you need “is this term significant?” or “which of these models should I report?”, the mgcv backend answers directly.

Robustness and constraints. Conversely, the pygam backend owns two practical features mgcv does not: Huber-robust fitting (outlier-tolerant by design) and soft shape constraints (monotonic/convex/concave pushes). If your data has sensor glitches or physics demands a monotone dose–response, the pygam backend is the one with the knob. Both handle periodicity, differently: the pygam backend wraps its basis and uses a circular difference penalty; the mgcv backend uses a purpose-built cyclic cubic basis.

Speed and scaling. With few terms and a small grid the pygam backend is effectively instant; its cost grows with the product of grid sizes and the number of \(\lambda\) slots, which is why the two-phase QR-caching matters. The mgcv backend’s cost is dominated by the optimiser: typically 10–100 objective evaluations, each one Cholesky — flat in the number of grid points, but sequential. In practice: pygam wins for sweeping many configurations; mgcv wins for a single many-termed fit with automatically tuned \(\lambda\) per term.

The deep difference in one sentence. The pygam backend asks “which of these :math:`lambda` candidates predicts best out of sample?” (GCV over a grid); the mgcv backend asks “which :math:`lambda` makes the data most likely under a smoothness prior?” (REML over a continuous parameter). Everything else — bases, solvers, covariances — follows from that choice of question.

Which backend should I use?¶

  • You want p-values, an R-style summary, or parity with R mgcv → backend='mgcv' with default REML.

  • You need automatic per-term smoothing with many terms → mgcv’s optimisation scales better than a per-term grid.

  • You want monotonic/convex/concave pushes or Huber robustness → backend='pygam'; these features don’t exist in the mgcv backend.

  • You want to sweep basis counts and smoothing parameters and inspect the GCV surface → pygam’s grid search, threaded.

  • You want the simplest possible mental model (one basis, one penalty, one criterion) → pygam.

  • You’re teaching GAMs → pygam for the machinery, then mgcv for the statistics; this chapter is laid out in that order.

When in doubt, fit both and compare: the decomposition plots and the fitted curves should agree on the data’s shape even where the p-values and \(\lambda\) philosophies differ. Disagreement between the two engines on the same data is a signal worth investigating — usually it means under-smoothing by GCV, an outlier distorting the unrobust mgcv fit, or a basis count too small for the grid being searched.

Key takeaways¶

Concept

One-sentence summary

Additive structure

Every prediction is a sum of independent, plottable pieces (both backends)

B-spline basis (pygam)

Build any smooth curve from localised LEGO-brick basis functions

Penalty (both)

Charge a tax for wiggles; let data pay it only when worthwhile

\(\lambda\) (both)

The tax rate: 0 = unpenalised, infinity = straight line

EDF (both)

How many “effective parameters” the penalty allows the model to use

GCV (pygam; mgcv option)

Approximate leave-one-out CV in a single fit; the pygam model-selection compass

REML (mgcv default)

The restricted likelihood with the penalty as a prior; the mgcv model-selection compass

SVD solver (pygam)

Numerically stable solution without squaring condition numbers

QR + Cholesky (mgcv)

Compact, fast solves; \(\log|H|\) and EDF fall out of the Cholesky factor

Basis zoo (mgcv)

tp/ts, cr/cs, cc, ps, re — different penalties and null spaces for different jobs

Sum-to-zero (mgcv)

Absorbed into the basis, so every smooth is centred by construction

Wood F-tests (mgcv)

Approximate per-term significance tests with p-values

Shape constraints (pygam)

Soft monotonic/convex/periodic pushes via the choice of penalty

Huber IRLS (pygam)

Down-weight outliers so they don’t hijack the curve

Grid search (pygam)

Two-phase QR+Cholesky: precompute K-dim work, then evaluate all lambdas in parallel

Comparison rule of thumb

mgcv for inference and automatic \(\lambda\); pygam for constraints, robustness, and fast sweeps
